  "text": "The piano tuner arrived carrying a bag no larger than a lunchbox.

“I was expecting more equipment,” Ruth said.

“Most people do.”

She led him into the front room. Someone had moved the piano away from the wall, leaving two shallow tracks in the carpet. On top stood a lamp and a birthday card from April.

“When was it last tuned?”

“My husband dealt with that.”

The tuner set his bag on the floor.

“Roughly?”

“Before the hospital.”

He nodded without asking which hospital, or when.

Ruth took the birthday card into the kitchen. She put the kettle on, then off again.

From the front room came a single note, repeated until it seemed less like music than someone trying a locked door.

Her husband had played on Sunday mornings. Usually the same few pieces, usually stopping in the same place to turn back a page.

“Do you play?” the tuner called.

“No.”

A pause.

“Will someone be using it?”

“My granddaughter might.”

Ruth had not asked her granddaughter.

When he finished, he played a short run of notes and closed his bag.

“There’s one key that may stick in damp weather.”

“Which one?”

He showed her. She pressed it with her forefinger.

“That was always troublesome,” she said.

“I can come back and look at the action.”

“Not yet.”

After he left, Ruth replaced the lamp but left the card in the kitchen.

She sat on the piano stool. Beneath the lid, the keys were clean except for a faint yellow mark near the middle.

She tried the troublesome note again.

This time it came back up."
